_comment: SKILL BLUEPRINT — output of the Spec agent, input to the Generator agent. One blueprint per standard.
subject: math
description: Students prove and apply the core triangle theorems: the measures of the interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$ (and the exterior-angle theorem that follows from it); the base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent (and its converse); the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, that the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length; and the Concurrency of Medians Theorem, that the three medians meet at a single point (the centroid) which divides each median in a $2{:}1$ ratio. Students both build the deductive arguments (two-column, paragraph, or flow proofs that cite definitions, the Parallel Postulate, alternate-interior-angle and corresponding-angle relationships, the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, and properties of congruent triangles) and use the theorems numerically to find unknown angle measures, segment lengths, and coordinates.
subSkills: Apply the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem to find a missing interior angle, setting up and solving $m\angle A + m\angle B + m\angle C = 180^\circ$
Apply the Exterior Angle Theorem, that an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, to find unknown measures
Prove the Triangle Angle-Sum Theorem by constructing a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and using alternate-interior angles
Identify base angles and the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle and apply the Base Angles Theorem (and its converse) to find missing angles or to conclude sides are congruent
Set up and solve algebraic equations from isosceles-triangle angle or side relationships
Apply the Triangle Midsegment Theorem to find a midsegment length, a third-side length, or to justify that a midsegment is parallel to the third side
Apply the Median Concurrency (centroid) Theorem, using the $2{:}1$ ratio in which the centroid divides each median to find segment lengths along a median
Find the centroid of a triangle from vertex coordinates using $\left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2+y_3}{3}\right)$
Write a two-column, paragraph, or flow proof of a triangle theorem, citing the appropriate definitions, postulates, and prior theorems with valid reasons

problemArchetypes.name: Angle-sum computation
problemArchetypes.example: In triangle $ABC$, $m\angle A = 53^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 78^\circ$. Find $m\angle C$.

problemArchetypes.name: Exterior angle theorem
problemArchetypes.example: An exterior angle at vertex $C$ of triangle $ABC$ measures $130^\circ$. If $m\angle A = 55^\circ$, find $m\angle B$.

problemArchetypes.name: Isosceles base angles
problemArchetypes.example: In isosceles triangle $PQR$, $PQ = PR$ and the vertex angle $m\angle P = 46^\circ$. Find the measure of each base angle.

problemArchetypes.name: Algebraic isosceles relationship
problemArchetypes.example: In isosceles triangle $DEF$, $DE = DF$. If $m\angle E = (3x + 8)^\circ$ and $m\angle F = (5x - 12)^\circ$, solve for $x$ and find $m\angle E$.

problemArchetypes.name: Midsegment length and parallelism
problemArchetypes.example: In triangle $ABC$, $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$. If $BC = 18$, find $MN$ and state its relationship to $\overline{BC}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Centroid 2:1 ratio
problemArchetypes.example: In triangle $ABC$, the medians meet at centroid $G$. Median $\overline{AD}$ has $AG = 10$. Find $GD$ and the full length $AD$.

problemArchetypes.name: Centroid from coordinates
problemArchetypes.example: Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(-2, 1)$, $B(4, 3)$, and $C(1, -7)$. Find the coordinates of the centroid.

problemArchetypes.name: Two-column or paragraph proof
problemArchetypes.example: Given triangle $ABC$ with $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$, prove that $\angle B \cong \angle C$ (Base Angles Theorem), justifying each step with a definition, postulate, or theorem.

Easy.description: Single-step application of one theorem with the relationship handed to the student and integer values. Substitute into the angle-sum equation and solve, read off congruent base angles, halve a side for a midsegment, or apply the $2{:}1$ centroid ratio in one move. One theorem, one computation, no algebra beyond a single subtraction or halving.
constraints: Exactly one theorem applied, named or obvious from the figure
Angle measures are integers and only one angle is unknown
Isosceles problems give the vertex angle or one base angle directly
Midsegment problems give the third side (find the midsegment) or vice versa with even integers
Centroid problems give one of the two median pieces and ask for the other using the $2{:}1$ ratio
No proof writing; at most identifying a single reason

Medium.description: Two coordinated steps or a one-variable equation. Use the exterior-angle theorem, set up and solve an isosceles relationship of the form $ax + b = cx + d$ or $2(\text{base}) + \text{vertex} = 180^\circ$, combine the angle-sum with isosceles base-angle congruence, find a centroid from coordinates, or complete a short fill-in-the-reason proof. Requires choosing the correct theorem and doing genuine algebra.
constraints: Two theorems combined, or a linear equation in one variable to solve
Isosceles items use algebraic expressions for angles or sides, or require the angle-sum to find the vertex from base angles
Centroid-from-coordinates and exterior-angle items belong here
May include a 2 to 3 step fill-in-the-blank (statements or reasons) proof
Answers may be fractions or non-integer coordinates, given as exact values

Hard.description: Multi-step synthesis or a full self-authored proof. Chain several theorems (e.g. midsegment plus angle-sum, or centroid ratio combined with an algebraic equation across two medians), prove a theorem from scratch in two-column or paragraph form with fully justified reasons, or solve a multi-figure problem where the output of one theorem is the input to another.
constraints: Three or more linked steps, or a complete original proof with every reason justified
Proof tasks must cite definitions, the Parallel Postulate, alternate-interior or corresponding angle relationships, the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, or congruent-triangle criteria correctly
May combine midsegment parallelism with angle relationships, or set two centroid segment expressions equal and solve
Algebra may involve solving for a variable then back-substituting into a second relationship

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: If split into two worksheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium computational fluency with the four theorems, angle-sum and exterior-angle, isosceles base angles (numeric and simple algebraic), midsegment length and parallelism, and the centroid 2:1 ratio and centroid-from-coordinates. tier2 covers Medium to Hard, multi-theorem synthesis problems and the proof-writing tasks (Triangle Angle-Sum proof, Base Angles Theorem proof, Midsegment Theorem reasoning). No item overlap between tiers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Thinks the interior angles of a triangle sum to $360^\circ$ instead of $180^\circ$, confusing it with a quadrilateral or full turn
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $m\angle A = 53^\circ$, $m\angle B = 78^\circ$, gives $m\angle C = 360 - 53 - 78 = 229^\circ$ instead of $180 - 53 - 78 = 49^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Applies the exterior angle theorem by including all three interior angles, or treats the exterior angle as supplementary to the wrong angle
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Sets the $130^\circ$ exterior angle equal to $m\angle A$ alone, giving $m\angle B = 130 - 55 - 55$, instead of $130^\circ = m\angle A + m\angle B$ so $m\angle B = 75^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is congruent to the base angles, or that all three angles are equal
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For vertex angle $46^\circ$, reports each base angle as $46^\circ$ instead of $\dfrac{180 - 46}{2} = 67^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to divide the remaining angle measure between the two base angles, assigning the full remainder to one base angle
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For vertex angle $46^\circ$, gives a base angle of $180 - 46 = 134^\circ$ instead of $67^\circ$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Doubles the midsegment to get the third side but reverses it, or sets the midsegment equal to the third side, ignoring the half-length relationship
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $BC = 18$, gives midsegment $MN = 36$ or $MN = 18$ instead of $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}(18) = 9$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Splits each median in half (1:1) or uses the wrong part of the $2{:}1$ ratio, mixing up the longer vertex-to-centroid segment with the shorter centroid-to-midpoint segment
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $AG = 10$ on median $\overline{AD}$, gives $GD = 10$ or $GD = 20$ instead of $GD = \dfrac{1}{2}(10) = 5$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Computes the centroid by averaging only two of the three vertices, or adds coordinates without dividing by 3
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $A(-2,1)$, $B(4,3)$, $C(1,-7)$, gives $(3, -3)$ (sum without dividing) instead of $\left(\dfrac{-2+4+1}{3}, \dfrac{1+3-7}{3}\right) = (1, -1)$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: In a proof, cites the conclusion as a reason or skips the justifying postulate, treating 'it looks congruent' or an unstated assumption as a valid reason
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Justifies $\angle B \cong \angle C$ by 'given' or 'they appear equal' instead of citing the Isosceles Triangle (Base Angles) Theorem or the congruent-triangle correspondence

_comment_itemCounts: worksheet.single = one ramped sheet (Easy->Hard across 15 items). tier1/tier2 only if the standard is split into two worksheets (15 each, no overlap).
